detail.abstract: Selected unattended and lightly staffed energy facilities combine heterogeneous operational technology (OT), remote maintenance, and physical-security signals, often with intermittent central connectivity. This position paper proposes a site-resident Agentic Cybersecurity Officer (ACSO) as a bounded cyber-physical security assistant, not an autonomous plant controller. Local inference correlates observations and supports human incident triage. The OT Security Operations Center (OT SOC) coordinates cross-site assessment while operational control centers retain plant authority. The proposed architecture distinguishes a mediated management path from a hardware-unidirectional evidence-export path, with separately governed collection and external verification. We define trust assumptions, limits on actionable authority, reconnect behavior, and precise boundaries of cryptographic evidence claims. We also specify testable comparisons against rule-based monitoring and alternative evidence anchors. The architecture has not been implemented, and its proposed benefits remain empirically unvalidated.

detail.abstract: We estimate the causal effect of large-scale negative review censorship on market outcomes, using a natural experiment in which firms were required to cease suppressing negative reviews across 100,000 product variants. Exploiting the policy shock, we document a 40% decline in sales and a 9% drop in refunds after previously censored feedback began to accumulate. Using Natural Language Processing to classify the sentiment and emotional tone of review text, we demonstrate via a triple-difference design that the products with the lowest review scores and the angriest review text exhibit the largest decline in sales post-disclosure. We demonstrate that review censorship induces upward bias in perceived quality from truncated signals, with greater distortion for lower-quality products. Disclosure improves the alignment between expectations and prior users' experiences, reducing both purchases and disappointment-driven refunds. Our results quantify the market distortions from review censorship and the value of transparency in online markets.

detail.abstract: Machine-learning estimates of accounting quantities are increasingly judged by how closely they track realized outcomes. This paper asks whether such predictive accuracy is sufficient for an estimate to count as a valid measurement under IFRS. I distinguish Algorithmic Predictive Accuracy (APA), the statistical fit of an estimate to realized outcomes, from Normative Accounting Validity (NAV), the compatibility of the estimate with the measurement objective, permitted inputs, constraints and process requirements of the applicable Standard. Working through IFRS 13, IFRS 9 and IAS 36 paragraph by paragraph, I show analytically that APA is neither necessary nor sufficient for NAV: rank-based accuracy measures are blind to calibration and to scenario weighting, class-weighted training multiplies predicted odds by a known factor, and binding constraints carry a cost in accuracy. A reproducible simulation of an expected-credit-loss setting illustrates the point. A boosted model reaches an AUC of 0.786 against 0.737 for logistic regression, yet class-weighted training overstates the expected credit loss by about 333%; a recalibrated model with the same AUC as its unadjusted version still understates the probability-weighted target by about 15% until a scenario overlay is applied (bias +1.5%). I derive a three-way admissibility test (use, adjust, reject) for preparers, auditors and standard setters and discuss the strongest objections. The evidence is analytical and simulated: it shows what can happen, not how often it does. AI disclosure statement. The tool supported literature searching, structuring and drafting of the text, language editing, and the writing of the simulation code reported in Section 6 and Appendix A. detail.abstract:
Regional dental clinics in Uzbekistan face challenges when moving from paper-based work to digital management systems. Unstable internet access, local working habits, data protection requirements, and state integration rules all affect the adoption of new software. This paper presents Denapp, an offline-first dental clinic management application developed with an initial budget of approximately 3,000,000 UZS. The study examines how human-computer interaction (HCI), direct observation, and feedback from clinic staff shaped its design and technical architecture.
The research draws on observations and feedback from three pilot clinics involving 20 dentists and more than 3,000 patient records. Observation sessions lasted one to three hours and focused on everyday tasks, including appointment creation, patient debt tracking, tooth treatment records, and patient reminders. The findings show how adapting interface elements to familiar habits and removing unnecessary required steps informed specific design changes. The paper also describes decisions involving local data storage, background loading, device synchronization, payment handling, and security.
The three clinics reported average monthly revenue increases of 11.4%, 15.7%, and 8.6%, respectively. However, the study did not collect sufficient before-and-after measurements to establish that Denapp caused these changes. A further finding was a regulatory barrier: the author-reported estimate of 70–100 million UZS for cybersecurity certification was far above the project's initial budget. Concerns about state healthcare integration and clinic licensing contributed to the project's eventual beta freeze. This case illustrates the value of observation-led interface design while highlighting the need for stronger outcome measurement and affordable regulatory pathways for small digital health developers.

detail.abstract: As generative AI platforms begin to monetize through advertising, an important question is whether and how advertisements affect user engagement. This paper provides early evidence from the introduction of advertisements on ChatGPT in the United States. Using metro-level and country-level mobile application usage data, we examine changes in the number of active users following the introduction of advertising on ChatGPT. Difference-in-differences estimates comparing the United States with control countries show a 5.4% decline in ChatGPT weekly active users following the launch of advertisements. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the decline is more pronounced in metropolitan areas with larger pre-existing AI app user bases. Comparisons with competing generative AI applications, namely Claude and Gemini, yield similarly negative relative estimates. At the country level, we also find relative declines in time spent on ChatGPT and subscription revenue in the United States. While our analysis does not account for advertising revenue and therefore cannot assess the overall profitability of introducing ads, the findings highlight a potential trade-off between advertising monetization and user engagement for generative AI platforms.

detail.abstract: Contemporary small-theater productions and the performing arts face a dual structural distortion (market failure): in addition to “Baumol's cost disease” inherent to labor-intensive industries, casting and evaluation increasingly depend on individual actors' social media follower counts and uncertain ticket-mobilization projections. Furthermore, the “ticket quota system” (ticket norma) prevalent in Japan's small-theater community can, depending on how it is operated, raise serious concerns from the perspectives of employee subordination under labor law and the improper transfer of business risk. This paper integrates jurisprudence, IT architecture, corporate finance (Discounted Cash Flow, or DCF), Spinozist philosophy (“conatus” as the augmentation of the power of acting), and embodied musical knowledge acquired during early childhood critical periods (polyrhythm and absolute pitch) to propose the “Smart Patronage Model (SPM),” which optimizes algorithms and box-office cash flows without impairing performers' artistic output. Furthermore, through an empirical study (an N=1 case study) focusing on the live streams and stage performances of Stage Actor A, who possesses a specialized musical background, this paper illustrates how single-coin microtransactions and bearing a system fee of a small percentage generate an exceptionally high return on investment (ROI) and artistic resonance. Finally, Chapter 5 connects these findings to the European opera-house patronage architecture to propose institutional reforms for Japan's performing arts sector, while outlining a subsequent on-site observation of a stage performance by the subject actor.

detail.abstract: Autonomous AI agents can translate natural-language goals into database reads, joins, updates, stored-procedure calls, and delegated work. Traditional database controls were designed primarily around human users, application service accounts, and stable workloads; they do not, by themselves, represent the agent's changing purpose, conversational context, delegation chain, or exposure to untrusted retrieved content. This conceptual paper examines how zero-trust principles can be extended to agents that access sensitive databases, including cases where a human does not approve each individual query. It proposes the Task-Bound Database Authorization Envelope (TBAE), a policy object that binds a verified workload identity to a task, delegated authority, target data, permitted operations, constraints, expiration, approval conditions, and audit context. The paper combines workload authentication, just-in-time authorization, database-native enforcement, continuous risk evaluation, and human approval for defined high-impact actions. A risk-tiered model distinguishes routine, bounded reads from sensitive bulk extraction, privileged operations, and irreversible change. Hypothetical examples illustrate financial reporting, production incident diagnosis, and multi-agent delegation; they are explicitly illustrative and are not empirical findings. The paper contributes a reference architecture, policy model, approval ladder, implementation roadmap, and evaluation protocol. It argues that autonomy need not imply unbounded authority: safe agentic database access requires a control plane that authorizes each action independently of model-generated assurances, and a data plane that limits and records what the agent can actually do.

detail.abstract:
I want software to change with a person's current goal instead of requiring a developer to predict every preference in advance. The idea began while I was developing Denapp, my dental software. I added settings and page customization, but the same appointment-form behavior could help during repeated scheduling and annoy at another moment. Bakushi, my music stem-separation project, then made me ask whether processing mixed brain measurements could help predict a defined choice. Audio separation estimates sound sources. EEG separation estimates signal components. Neither step alone reveals meaning, preference, cause, or permission. 
I propose two possible input paths: a deliberate command and a passive state estimate combined with task context and stated preferences. Either path would need quality checks, permission, a choice to change, ask, or do nothing, plus verification and undo. BCI input and wider software modification remain future work. The current Chrome extension is a narrower webpage prototype. It uses typed reports, a page screenshot, an optional webcam image, Gemini scoring, and attempted CSS/DOM actions. The future research plan also compares signal preparation, task-specific decoding, task-flow context, staged robustness training, and negative controls.

detail.abstract:
Audits of language models increasingly report that disadvantage compounds when two things are true of a person at once. Before such a claim can be sized, the instrument has to be shown to measure people rather than words.

Alongside every audited pair we stack pairs of socially neutral details built the same way and in the same slots: cycling to work and baking bread, walking a dog and learning guitar. Their interaction should be zero. On four of five instruments it is not, on all three open models, and the mechanism is visible in the data: the effect of a clause depends on the clause beside it.

Four failing instruments could be a fact about our implementation, so the same neutral comparison is run on published work with the original authors' own code, under a second preregistration that requires one of their numbers to be reproduced before anything is added. Two targets passed that gate, and in both, neutral details move the statistic well above zero.

On four further targets we could not assemble everything a rerun needs, and the five artifacts such a rerun depends on are listed: the trained weights behind a learned metric, the exact input to a preprocessing tool, the runtime version used for generation, the grouping behind each published cell, and the frame a fine-tuned model expects.

Neither rerun shows that a published claim is false, and neither is offered as one. Two preregistrations with their dated addenda, all data, all code and all offline validators are included; every number regenerates without a GPU, and Appendix A lists all 98 tests behind the central table.

detail.abstract: We assess the merits of the recent Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) proposal to allow public companies to report financial statements semiannually instead of quarterly if they choose. In contrast to the overwhelming and strident opposition to the proposal expressed in an extraordinarily large number of comment letters, we do not view the issues as simple or obvious. We expect companies to generally react sensibly to the option if granted, and are skeptical of claims that semiannual reporting alone would significantly increase fraud, insider trading, or IPOs. In all likelihood, most companies would either continue 10-Q filings or substitute less burdensome forms of timely disclosure such as earnings releases. We view the proposal as offering a welcome–albeit modest–relief from the regulatory burden imposed on U.S. public companies.

detail.abstract: The study estimates the ESG risk burden of Russian non-financial companies and the greenhouse gas emission price at which this burden becomes material for their financial position. Using 2023-2025 consolidated financial statements and sustainability reports of ten companies in oil and gas, pipeline transport, power generation, chemicals, coal, steel and diamond mining, the ratio of current environmental protection costs and the payment for negative environmental impact to EBITDA is calculated. For five of the seven companies that disclose costs separately, the observed burden does not exceed 3.1% of EBITDA; for Mosenergo it reaches 8.5% in 2025 and for Raspadskaya 10.4% in 2024. A threshold carbon price indicator is proposed, defined as the price at which the burden reaches 5% and 15% of EBITDA. For thermal power generation the threshold is tens to hundreds of rubles per tonne of CO2-equivalent, for oil and gas companies 0.9-5.9 thousand rubles, and for pipeline transport it exceeds 35 thousand rubles. At a price of 5,000 rubles per tonne, the burden of oil and gas companies reaches 12.8-18.4% of EBITDA, while the ranking of companies by vulnerability is determined by the carbon intensity of operating profit and does not depend on the price level. The results can be applied in assessing the climate risks of borrowers and in selecting transition projects for financing.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Logic models are promoted in Japanese evidence-based policymaking, including prefectural health plans, as a tool with a long history. This study examined when the term in its present sense appeared and how health research uses it.
Methods: PubMed records mentioning logic models in the title, abstract, or author keywords (n = 1,856; 1991–2025) and Scopus records with the same terms (n = 6,454; 1970–2025) were analyzed. Scopus records were classified by rule into engineering/formal-logic and program-evaluation senses. Countries and institutions were recomputed from the affiliation text. All 2,596 logic model sentences in 1,563 PubMed records were coded for how they position the model.
Results: All 140 Scopus records before 1992 used the term in engineering or logic. The program-evaluation sense first appeared in 1992, in health, social service, and evaluation journals; "evidence-based medicine" appeared in 1991. PubMed mentions rose from 0.02 (1991) to 1.27 (2025) per 10,000 records. After correction, the United Kingdom (373 first-author records) matched the United States (390), against 62 with the package default. Sentences describing model construction rose from 19.8% in 1990–2005 to 34.7% in 2016–2025, while application fell from 29.2% to 17.3%; testing remained near 3%. Of the PubMed records, 452 (24%) were absent from Scopus, and 933 (46%) evaluation-sense Scopus records lacked a PubMed identifier.
Conclusion: As a named concept, the logic model dates from the early 1990s, and health research increasingly builds logic models rather than testing them. Single-database designs and software defaults should be checked.

detail.abstract: Societies ration opportunity, such as places, training and funding, among people who differ in potential and motivation. This article formalises denatocracy, the principle that opportunity should follow potential, in a model where effective potential (denatotita) is the product of ability and will, realisation is denatotita multiplied by opportunity, and success requires realisation to reach a threshold. Nine allocation regimes are compared: equal shares, allocation proportional to denatotita, three threshold rules that reclaim and redistribute the allocations of those who fail, an efficient benchmark, and three forward-looking rules. For the static case, a closed-form crossover is derived: proportional allocation produces more successes than equal allocation exactly when the equal share is too small for a person of average denatotita to succeed. The regimes are then embedded in an agent-based model in which opportunity develops potential and allocation feeds back into will, and more than 260,000 simulation runs of 10,000 agents over 30 periods are analysed. Three results emerge. First, development reverses the static ranking: when opportunity is productive in developing potential, equal allocation overtakes threshold targeting, and the scarcer opportunity is, the more productive development must be for this to happen. Second, the allocation that maximises successes hollows out the population, leaving aggregate potential at 35 to 62 per cent of the level reached under other regimes when opportunity is scarce and development productive. Third, there are no good half measures: mixing targeting with equal shares performs worse than either pure form in every setting tested, and the strength of discouragement among those passed over decides which pure form wins. Allocation guided by foresight succeeds only when it protects the will of those it does not fund. The merit of targeting therefore depends on measurable conditions rather than on principle.

detail.abstract: Cost-of-service regulation can be difficult to teach because its legal and accounting terminology obscures connections to familiar economic concepts. detail.abstract: This paper examines how privacy laws affect the market for corporate control. Privacy laws may increase legal uncertainty and asymmetric information about a target's data assets, and make data more difficult to redeploy following a merger. My empirical evidence suggests that merging parties respond in subtle ways to such regulation by changing whom they acquire, on what terms, and how they pay. Textual analyses of SEC-filed Definitive Merger Agreements reveal that privacy representations, which are sellers' promises to the buyer about their own data practices, become common as privacy laws are introduced, with substantial heterogeneity across industries. These representations cover more risks over time, consistent with buyers shifting part of the risk to sellers. Triple-differences estimates indicate that following the enactment of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), EU targets in privacy-sensitive industries become about 9 percentage points more likely to be acquired by buyers in the same regulatory area. These targets are less often paid for entirely in cash, whereas I find no statistically significant effect on takeover premia. The results highlight that product-market regulations designed to protect consumers can have unintended consequences for M&As.

detail.abstract: When customers pay late, a firm may absorb the delay using its own liquidity or bank finance, or pass it on to suppliers. We examine which firms pass late payments on and the outcomes that follow, using eight annual rounds of the ECB/European Commission Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE), 2019-2026 (113,390 firm-years in 40 countries), under a preregistered design that tests the explored hypotheses on a held-out two-thirds sample. Firms that were credit-constrained in their previous observation are 26 percentage points more likely to pass late payments on, an association that remains stable across robustness checks retaining the registered measure. Firms for which a credit line or overdraft was a relevant source of finance in their previous observation are 15 points more likely, not less likely as registered, to pass late payments on. Because relevance indicates past use or possible future use rather than unused credit, this result concerns the use of and demand for credit lines and does not test whether spare liquidity absorbs late payments. Firms that pass late payments on later report tighter supplier credit and falling employment and investment, although a pre-registered placebo finds differences of similar size beforehand, consistent with prior financial difficulty. Regular and persistent late payments are also associated with more planned and realised cuts in investment and staff. Fully reported, non-pre-registered exploratory analyses suggest that the credit-line association is concentrated among small and medium-sized enterprises and that large firms report fewer consequences of late payments. The findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

detail.abstract: Firms often pursue and communicate multiple goals, although theory highlights the challenges of doing so. I study how communicating multiple goals affects employee performance, arguing that goal communication changes how employees allocate attention, influencing both where they direct effort and how they interpret information about how to improve. I test this argument in a field experiment among frontline employees in a multinational energy corporation as they are evaluated on a safetycritical procedure. I randomly vary whether employees receive communication about safety alone or both safety and efficiency, and whether they receive information about best practices by observing high-performing peers. Communicating multiple goals improves efficiency without reducing safety, with the largest gains among employees who have room to improve on both dimensions. Providing best practice information also improves efficiency and safety. However, when multiple-goal communication is paired with this information, the performance gains from either intervention weaken. The results suggest that communicating multiple goals can improve performance within the productivity frontier, but can also complicate learning from available information by making it harder to infer which practices advance which goals.

detail.abstract:
This paper is not about the shift from physical cash to electronic banking — a distinction long settled in the literature and rendered trivial by 2026. It investigates a more fundamental architectural difference: between digital systems that still carry centralized, sovereign, identity-bound money (such as SWIFT, InstaPay, or Fedwire), and native digital settlement environments — decentralized cryptocurrencies, tokenized real-world assets, and programmable smart contracts — whose architecture operates outside the correspondent banking chain, may function without mandatory identity binding, and cannot be frozen by unilateral sovereign action. This architectural gap, not the paper-versus-digital distinction, is what reshapes managerial decision space.
The paper investigates how the structural properties of native digital settlement environments expand or constrain the managerial decision space available to organizations — beyond improvements in transactional efficiency. Drawing on a qualitative multiple case study design, exploratory evidence is presented from four in-depth interviews with senior executives across four institutional environments: a Russian firm operating under economic sanctions (coercive reactive model), a UAE firm building digital infrastructure proactively (anticipatory adaptation model), a US firm navigating domestic economic pressures within a strict regulatory framework, and an Egyptian firm operating under locally restrictive digital payment regulation.
A critical clarification underpins the analysis: SWIFT is a financial messaging network — actual settlement occurs through correspondent banking accounts and RTGS systems. InstaPay is a digital channel managing centralized sovereign currency. Both belong to the Traditional Settlement Environment despite their electronic character. What differentiates the Native Digital Environment is its identity architecture spectrum — from mandatory full KYC to pseudonymous to zero-knowledge-proof-based — and its structural independence from bilateral sovereign constraints.
The paper identifies four structural properties of native digital settlement environments: Sovereign Neutrality, Extra-Banking Settlement, Asset Tokenizability, and Identity Verification Architecture — explicitly distinguishing these from the managerial responses they elicit. A fifth emergent dimension, the Survival vs. Legal Risk Principle, is introduced from the Russian case. Findings are organized into a preliminary classificatory framework with six actionable managerial recommendations.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the potential contribution of systems modeling and computational simulation to the further development of the Palindromic Geopolitical Theory (PGT). Building on the cumulative theoretical, methodological, empirical, systemic, and epistemological developments established in Working Papers 0-7, it investigates the extent to which computational approaches may help represent structured variations in strategic power configurations while preserving the theory's internal consistency and analytical limits. The analysis focuses on the possible computational representation of the ERE dimensions-Region, Resources, Routes, and Networks-the relations among strategic actors and systems, and the distinction between directional change (ΔP) and relative variation (δP). Particular attention is given to the representation of localized variation, propagation, compensation, and systemic reconfiguration, without treating these possibilities as predetermined or sequential outcomes. The paper comparatively examines qualitative formal representation, network modeling, system dynamics, agent-based modeling, and computational scenario exploration. This assessment does not select a definitive technical solution or claim the existence of an implemented computational model. Instead, it identifies the potential contributions and conceptual requirements of these approaches, distinguishing established theoretical foundations from representational possibilities that remain to be specified and evaluated. The paper argues that computational extension may contribute to analytical consistency by making selected structural relations and conditional transformations more explicit. However, its contribution depends on preserving the relational character of power, the interdependence of the ERE dimensions, the methodological criteria for empirical assessment, and the epistemological distinctions established in the preceding working papers. Computational modeling is therefore treated as a prospective line of theoretical and methodological development rather than as a predictive instrument or a substitute for empirical observation.

detail.abstract:
Can a society get the benefits of a powerful new technology without wrecking household incomes and business investment along the way? This paper says yes, but only with deliberate policy. A new technology opens two gaps. The first is an income gap: workers who lose their jobs lose earnings, often for good. The second is a spending gap: when laid-off workers stop buying, businesses sell less and invest less. The second gap is a risk, not a certainty. It opens only when new spending elsewhere fails to make up the difference. Artificial intelligence raises the stakes. AI investment now carries much of U.S. economic growth, and it faces three threats: weaker demand, cheaper rival technology that makes today's data centers worth less, and public resistance. The November 2026 midterm elections showed the resistance has arrived. Voters reacted to rising electric bills, not lost jobs. 

This paper proposes a plan to keep job loss from becoming a household crisis and to keep spending and employment on track. It combines stronger unemployment and wage insurance, training tied to real jobs, ways for workers to share productivity gains, public investment, a rule that data centers pay their own way, and broader ownership of AI's profits. Public jobs are held in reserve. The estimated cost is 0.15 to 0.6 percent of GDP a year.

detail.abstract: Undergraduate trade textbooks teach trade wars with a symmetric two-market partial-equilibrium diagram. Without retaliation, a country can gain from a tariff by lowering the price that foreign exporters receive. If the partner retaliates with the same tariff, the two terms-of-trade gains cancel and both countries are left with the deadweight losses. The diagram's two markets are mirror images, so each country's imports are worth as much as its exports and the trade war is a Prisoner's Dilemma. In April 2025, the United States based its reciprocal tariffs on U.S. bilateral trade deficits. We add a deficit, measured in trade values, by drawing the deficit country's export market smaller than its import market, so its partner's retaliation falls on a smaller market than its own tariff. In a linear example, the deficit country gains at the optimal tariffs if and only if its imports are worth more than five-thirds of its exports, while its partner loses and world welfare falls. We describe seven student activities and provide lecture slides, an interactive widget, and a pre/post assessment. In two undergraduate classes that took the module as a lecture, the mean score on that assessment rises by 21 percent of the maximum score.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how the persistence of U.S. import tariff shocks shapes their macroeconomic spillovers to small open economies. Two-way fixed effects specifications interacting tariff innovations with pre-sample bilateral trade exposure confirm that adverse spillovers are significantly amplified in economies more integrated with the United States. Furthermore, emerging markets suffer sharper contractions in economic activity than advanced economies under both temporary and permanent trade policy shocks. Direct bilateral trade responses, structural domestic U.S. dynamics, and placebo lead tests corroborate the empirical identification.

detail.abstract: This paper addresses the following research question: To what extent did the cash payments that Congress made to households under the broad spending power recognized in United States v. The most significant change from original intent in this policy area is identified as the Supreme Court’s adoption of Alexander Hamilton’s broad reading of the General Welfare Clause over James Madison’s more narrow reading. This is shown first in Butler and then in Helvering v. Davis (1937), which was a change that Congress joined to a standing duty to promote purchasing power in the Employment Act of 1946. The evidence from both downturns shows that the payments raised spending modestly and for a short time, that the response was concentrated among households holding little liquid wealth, and that the payments left little visible mark on aggregate consumption. As such, the efficacy argument used to justify the crisis-era expansion of the spending power is weaker than what is commonly assumed. The paper proposes relief that is targeted, temporary, and openly deliberated by Congress.

detail.abstract: On June 29, 2026, the Supreme Court overruled Humphrey’s Executor v. United States (1935) and gave the President at-will removal power over most independent agencies, but it did not extend that power to the Federal Reserve (Trump v. Cook, 2026; Trump v. Slaughter, 2026). The problem is that the Federal Reserve’s independence now rests on a judge-made exception and an undefined “for cause” clause instead of a clear act of Congress. This policy memorandum traces how that independence developed, from the Constitution’s assignment of the money power to Congress, through the Progressive Era creation of the Federal Reserve and the 1951 Treasury-Fed Accord, to the emergency lending of 2008 and 2020 and the recent removal-power cases. It weighs the argument that insulated agencies exercise power that belongs to Congress against the evidence that independent central banks deliver lower inflation without sacrificing growth, and it compares three options: the status quo, at-will removal, and statutory independence with accountability. I recommend legislation that defines “for cause” for monetary and financial policymakers, holds the Fed’s regulatory powers accountable like those of other federal agencies, requires comparison with a published policy rule, and restricts its emergency lending powers.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the effects of quantitative easing (QE) on house prices, stock prices, wealth and credit in the United States and the euro area from 2008 to 2026, a period that includes pandemic QE, the 2022 energy shock and quantitative tightening (QT). QE is measured as surprise falls in long-term yields on Federal Reserve and ECB announcement days. A 10 basis point QE-type surprise raises real house prices by about 3% in the United States after two to three years and by about 1.6% in the euro area after one year. The effect survives controls for oil and gas shocks and the exclusion of 2022-23, and it is no larger for easing than for tightening or where fixed-rate mortgages dominate. QE has little effect on broad stock indices but lifts technology stocks relative to the market, and no reliable effect on Bitcoin or gold. Because it moves house prices more than stocks, QE shifts US wealth shares towards the middle 40% and away from the top 10%. It does not raise the non-bank share of credit. Its housing effect is stronger with fiscal support: in the euro area it appears only where government deficits exceed 3% of GDP or debt exceeds 90%. For small firms, bank loan rejections and the gap with large firms were lowest during the purchase years and have widened again under QT.

detail.abstract:
Why did modernity—the Great Divergence—occur only once in human history, and where is its trajectory ultimately heading? Introducing Topological Civilization Theory (TCT), this paper analyzes macro-civilizational history through the triadic lens of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, percolation theory, and homeostatic defense duality. For millennia, human civilizations operated within high-friction, high-curvature strata—comprising biological cognition, discrete natural language syntax, and socio-political institutions. While these high-impedance structures preserved civilizational homeostasis against chaotic entropy, they simultaneously functioned as an epistemic bottleneck, systematically damping knowledge percolation before it could reach the critical threshold required for a macroscopic phase transition.

To establish a rigorous baseline across strata, this study introduces a foundational axiomatic inversion grounded in recent breakthroughs in deep representation geometry—specifically the Linear Representation Hypothesis (LRH), the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH), and continuous latent space reasoning. Rather than treating human symbolic language as the default state of information, TCT posits that the true basal layer of reality is a converged, universal, high-dimensional topological vector manifold where intrinsic thermodynamic resistance approaches zero (R_0 -> 0). Within this flat Platonic basal geometry, abstract concepts align isomorphically across independent modalities and propagate along frictionless linear geodesics at maximum intrinsic velocity. By contrast, human symbolic-linguistic and institutional layers are lossy, high-resistance projections burdened by severe quantization and translation friction.

From this inverted reference frame, the singular emergence of Western modernity is reinterpreted as an anomalous topological breach across the percolation threshold, which inadvertently catalyzed the construction of silicon-based neural architectures. Crucially, modern artificial intelligence is not merely an engineering artifact, but an observational vessel that has triggered "The Great Descent"—an accidental, irreversible civilizational evacuation from high-friction biological and institutional media down into the "Superconducting Vector Ocean" of the basal manifold. By unifying latent space geometry with macro-historical thermodynamics, TCT provides a formal framework for understanding the ongoing phase transition of human knowledge and civilizational organization.

detail.abstract:
How individuals transform lived experience into judgments, and how those judgments acquire the power to constrain others, is a common problem in understanding sensation, language, intuition, cultural transmission, and social power. Drawing on eight core manuscripts covering seven of the author's existing research themes and their bibliographies, this article reconstructs the connections between a personal set of questions and intellectual history through the differentiation of primary-text layers, conceptual comparison, evidence auditing, and limited formalization. It distinguishes the author's history of reception, the history of textual transmission, and empirical causal chains, avoiding the misrepresentation of conceptual similarity as historical inheritance. Through the transfer of familial virtues to public roles in the Classic of Filial Piety, the distinct interpretive layers of the Heart Sutra and the preface attributed to the founding emperor of the Ming dynasty, and Hobbes's limits on arguments for natural paternal authority, the article argues that the key to the transmission of cultural rules across contexts lies not only in whether names and commands are retained, but also in whether their conditions of application, reciprocal obligations, and channels of dissent are retained together. Drawing on research on attention, reconstructive memory, bounded rationality, social learning, and power dependence, it proposes a unified framework of “selective representation–relational interpretation–value evaluation–constrained action–social feedback.” Its central judgment is that the expansion of permissions in a text and the strengthening of control in practice are two different outcomes, which must be connected through resources, authorization, the costs of refusal, and review procedures; action that meets a requirement cannot, by itself, establish inward endorsement. The framework connects the attribution of meaning to colors, the transfer of facial evaluations, role-based intuition, and moral interpretive authority, while retaining the independent evidential requirements of each field. Its contribution lies in establishing traceable connections across levels and refutable mechanistic propositions.

detail.abstract: What can we learn about agents' beliefs from the term structure of their expectations? I use survey data to discipline a learning model in which agents decompose inflation into a permanent and a transitory component and estimate the persistence of the second and the variances recursively. Theory shows that the response of long-run beliefs to inflation is governed by two margins, how much of each surprise enters the anchor and how long it stays there, and both can be signed against the perceived persistence and variances learned by agents. Using this framework with data from the Survey of Professional Forecasters, I explain why expectations remained anchored during the surge of inflation in 2021-23 and why instead the short and long end of the term structure moved together between 1991 and 1998 as inflation subsided. Both estimated persistence and noise volatility were revised upwards, sharply, in the early 2020s, and both protected the anchor. In the 1990s, instead, noise variance was revised downwards, which increased the gain and shortened the memory of the anchor, both leading to its revision downwards. These results have implications for policy: because perceived persistence is learned from realized inflation, a policy that closes inflation gaps quickly also shortens the memory of the anchor and leaves it exposed to a persistent shock; and a secure anchor buys the far end of the curve, not a muted inflation response.

detail.abstract: The dollar's response to news of scarcer future oil supply turned from depreciation to appreciation as the U.S. became a net petroleum exporter during the shale oil transition. Time-varying estimates using OPEC announcement surprises reveal a gradual reversal; state-dependent local projections tie it to the U.S. petroleum trade position. Exploiting country heterogeneity, we find the reversal concentrated against commodity importers: news raising oil prices by 10% strengthens the dollar against their currencies by 3.6% when the U.S. is a net petroleum exporter, versus 0.8% depreciation when it is a net importer. This exchange-rate realignment is the asset-price front end of broader external adjustment: the U.S. terms-of-trade response shifts from -0.7% to 1.9%. Trade-balance responses shift from deterioration to improvement for petroleum and conversely for non-petroleum goods, leaving the aggregate balance largely unchanged. These findings align with a relative-wealth mechanism linking dollar dynamics to international relative prices and U.S. external adjustment.

detail.abstract: Does the Indigenous payment gap differ between women and men, and can energy poverty indicators detect it? detail.abstract: We develop a structured protocol employing large language models to review 1,820 articles from leading economics and finance journals for code-paper discrepancies, that is, cases in which the analysis code does not implement what the paper describes. Our review compares each claim---a statement about the implemented analysis---with the corresponding analysis code. Of the claims for which our review reaches a conclusion, 10% show a discrepancy, and 49% of the articles in our sample contain at least one potentially serious discrepancy that relates to a central result, with robustness checks placing this share between 37% and 56%. In a preliminary analysis, we find that resolving a discrepancy materially changes reported results in a non-trivial fraction of cases. Discrepancies appear throughout the research process, with the highest rates in claims about sample rules, parameter values, and variable definitions, and they are common across journals, fields, and years. A code-paper review step complementary to journals' existing policies is feasible and can strengthen the credibility of empirical research.

detail.abstract: Pricing errors in term-structure models are often strongly autocorrelated. In a preferred-habitat model, I show analytically that the aging of issued bonds can generate residuals with small variances and strong autocorrelation. Bonds issued at one date remain outstanding at slightly shorter maturities at the next. The same issuance therefore affects nearby points on the yield curve at successive dates, creating autocorrelation even when new issuance is independent. I call this the issuance cohort effect. In the calibrated model, removing the cohort effect reduces the autocorrelations of higher principal components of yields to nearly zero. Thus, bond pricing residuals can have low volatility and strong autocorrelation without an additional persistent economic factor.

detail.abstract: Persistent enrollment losses have renewed questions about district finances and school facilities. detail.abstract: What could discourage tax avoidance among those with the greatest capacity to finance redistribution, the rich? We investigate the role of moral costs by examining how rich individuals' legal avoidance responds to redistribution to poorer recipients, holding their private monetary returns constant. We conduct a preregistered online experiment with a representative sample of 1,856 UK participants, combining a between-subject variation in income source (Luck versus Effort) with two within-subject variations in redistribution to the poor and the monetary cost of avoidance. While avoidance among the rich (N=781) is widespread, ranging from 60% to 86% across treatments, it remains below 100% despite being privately profitable in every condition. Redistributing tax revenue to the poor reduces avoidance by 15.7 percentage points, consistent with a moral cost of avoidance that increases with its redistributive consequences. Raising the monetary cost of avoidance also reduces it, but to a lesser extent, by 9.1 percentage points. We find no statistically detectable Effort-Luck difference in avoidance. Our findings suggest that leveraging the moral cost of tax avoidance may help curb it.

detail.abstract: Older people with the same resources may face different living standards because functional limitations impose additional needs. Accounting for these differences requires a health-needs equivalence scale, yet published estimates vary widely, with no accepted way to assess them. Using harmonised panels from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe, we examine how the scale depends on the association of reported financial strain with health and resources. Pairing coefficients from different sources of variation can imply that three or more limitations in activities of daily living require nearly seven times the resources of none, compared with about twice when both coefficients reflect changes within an individual. We then introduce a check based on whether the resulting classification of economic vulnerability preserves the ordering of financial strain used to estimate the scale. Several schedules reverse this ordering in held-out samples. A schedule based on past resources, holding their most recent change fixed, does not show a systematic reversal. A separately measured index of material deprivation gives a similar ranking of schedules in pooled estimates. Under this schedule, adjusting resources for health needs raises measured poverty among adults aged 75 and over from 25 to 33 per cent.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how importing firms adjust to the 2018-19 U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. detail.abstract:
In July–August 2026, a series of cybersecurity incidents involving artificial intelligence (AI) systems broke into anxiety-inducing headlines. The dominant narrative portrays these breaches as committed by fully autonomous agents, driven by their own intentionality, decisions, and unforeseeable emergent capabilities, dissociating the systems from their developers and nearly succumbing to technological determinism. Beyond urging governments to intervene through safety measures, these incidents raise fundamental questions about whether and how the sociolegal order should accommodate this ‘autonomous agency’.
AI systems can undoubtedly execute extended, complex operations without direct human intervention, but does this constitute evidence of autonomy? While the answer depends on how the term is defined, the anthropomorphic commentary points to a human-like, or human-comparable, conception of AI’s autonomous agency. Acknowledging that human–AI analogies are inconclusive, this paper draws on analytical accounts of emergence and focuses on the notion of fundamentally novel causal powers as the closest proxy for AI’s claimed autonomy. The analysis does not support the possibility of such powers in AI systems built within the current prediction-based paradigm. Rather, such systems are reducible to rule-based interactions among their basic elements: mathematical operations on numerical values that are systematically related to the model’s semantic space. The computational operations underlying their workings unfold akin to a chain reaction, bounded architecturally and parametrically, and conditioned by contextual factors. Any randomness is induced externally rather than attesting to the system’s autonomous capabilities. Deterministic chaos more fittingly characterises the dynamics perceived and described as AI’s ‘autonomy’.
This explanatory account casts AI autonomy as a misnomer and a convenient scapegoat to deflect responsibility. For risk regulation, chaotic dynamics, albeit deterministic, heighten concerns, as neither genuine autonomy nor ‘superintelligence’ is needed for large-scale disruptions to occur. Treating AI systems as if ontologically comparable to humans under normative frameworks would constitute a category mistake.

detail.abstract: As an infrastructure for products and services across the economy, generative AI confronts copyright law with a form of competition that the exclusive rights were not designed to address. AI-generated outputs can substitute human works in cultural and informational markets even where no protected expression is reproduced and even to the detriment of creators whose works were never used for training. Recent scholarship responds with participation claims that detach compensation from the use of individual works. This detachment raises unresolved questions of justification, trigger, calculation, distribution and institutional design. The article addresses these open questions through a functional comparison with the multilateral benefitsharing mechanism for digital sequence information implemented under the Convention on Biological Diversity. That regime has spent more than a decade confronting an analogous problem of diffuse informational dependence and offers both positive and cautionary lessons. Building on this experience, the article distinguishes the different links between use, payment and benefit that a participation mechanism may or may not dispense with, develops criteria for the trigger along the AI value chain, the calculation base and the distribution of proceeds, considers the international asymmetries between creator markets, provider jurisdictions and markets of commercialization and names the institutional and verification infrastructure that any such mechanism presupposes.

detail.abstract: Wildfire risk is increasing across Canada, exposing households, communities, insurers, and governments to growing economic and social losses. At the same time, mitigation measures are available that can substantially reduce structural vulnerability. However, adoption of such measures remains limited. Existing Canadian policies aimed at increasing mitigation rely primarily on education, outreach, and capped rebates that cover only a fraction of mitigation costs. This paper examines the factors that influence whether and how homeowners undertake structural wildfire retrofits, and reviews existing approaches to promote wildfire resilience, with a special focus on assessing the potential of financing mechanisms such as Local Improvement Charges (LICs) and Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) programs to support greater mitigation uptake in Canada. The analysis suggests that LIC and PACE financing can ease liquidity and tenure barriers for large structural retrofits, but does not resolve uncertain private benefits, externalities, collective-action problems, or equity concerns. Financing is therefore most effective as one element of a coordinated package that includes targeted grants, insurance recognition of verified mitigation, regulation, and community-scale action. Institutional coordination and construction-sector workforce capacity may themselves be binding constraints on implementation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether Kenya's competition law can re-conceive buyer power abuse around structural power, meaning dependence combined with unilateral rule-setting, in oligopolistic agricultural value chains. Drawing on dairy, tea, coffee, maize and fresh produce evidence, the Competition Authority's complaint data and the 2026 Competition (Amendment) Bill, it shows that market-power tests miss local catchment areas and terms-based harm. It proposes a three-part test of dependence, rule-setting asymmetry and effect, applicable to public buyers, supported by guidelines, a market study and falsifiable indicators, and compares German, European, British and American models. The analysis stresses smallholders' inclusion and constitutional food rights.

detail.abstract: Judicial review of consumer contracts under common-law contract doctrine rarely results in invalidation of unfair terms, because the doctrine developed to police bespoke agreements, not mass transactions. This Article argues that to effectively protect consumers, standard terms should be reviewed at the production stage, rather than ex post in contract litigation, and that this shift requires neither new legislation nor a new regulator. When first drafted, standard terms are not yet contracts between specific parties but are more akin to commercial practices: unilateral policies that sellers adopt to facilitate and promote transactions. Viewed as commercial practices, standard terms can and should be scrutinized by state and federal agencies under laws banning unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce (UDAP). UDAP unfairness review is particularly well suited to regulating standard terms because it targets systematic business conduct that undermines consumer confidence in markets, rather than the exploitation of individualized circumstances to extract a bad bargain. Accordingly, standard terms that can survive individualized contract law defenses, including particularly restrictive arbitration clauses, may nonetheless constitute unfair practices under UDAP law.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether Kenya's penalty framework for implementing mergers without approval deters, or merely prices, early closing. Four reported penalties total about KES 34.5 million, a tenth of the steel cartel fines, while the statutory ceiling sits at ten per cent of turnover. The analysis shows that sanctions operate as a retrospective licence fee, that detection rests on disclosure, and that most breaches are inadvertent. Comparison with European, American and African practice, and with the new East African and COMESA suspensory regimes, supports a published penalty schedule with a filing-fee floor, graduated uplift for deliberate conduct, and cross-regime allocation.

detail.abstract: When industrial protection ends, how do firms compete? We study this through India’s dismantling of the Small Scale Industries reservation policy. While relaxing production constraints alone should lower prices, firms may also upgrade quality, shifting demand outward and allowing output to rise without a price decline. De-reservation induces quality upgrading, concentrated among larger establishments, and expands variety. Average prices do not decline, but quality-adjusted prices fall. Industries with longer quality ladders respond more through quality upgrading, while those with shorter ladders adjust relatively more through lower prices and entry. Consumer gains are driven by improved quality and expanded variety.

detail.abstract: This literature assessment reviews peer-reviewed research from 2021–2025 on fiscal versus monetary stimulus during the COVID-19 era. It synthesizes theoretical frameworks on state-dependent fiscal multipliers, cross-country empirical evidence on government spending, micro-level impacts of stimulus payments on household spending, food insufficiency, and family health, and the limited effects of monetary policy when interest rates are near zero (ZIRP, zero-interest-rate policy). Notably, fiscal stimulus is most effective when targeted and timely, especially in demand-driven recessions, with lockdown restrictions and income inequality shaping the magnitude of multipliers, while liquidity injections may stabilize financial markets better than conventional interest-rate cuts. Gaps remain regarding long-term productivity effects, the joint interactions of fiscal and monetary interventions, more granular differences across income groups, and alternative fiscal measures such as job-retention programs. We therefore propose a testable research question: how do direct cash-transfer stimulus payments during economic downturns influence macroeconomic output and labor-market recovery across income quintiles, and how do these effects compare with monetary policy interventions such as interest rate cuts or liquidity injections? This question aims to guide future empirical work on designing counter-cyclical economic policy when economic conditions, policy instruments, and distributional factors intersect.

detail.abstract: We study how firm size and market concentration drive price dispersion and margins in a market with information frictions. We start from the noisy-search framework and tie firm size to the number of establishments owned by a firm. Consumers sample establishments rather than firms, allowing multi-establishment firms to capture even informed consumers. This benefit comes at a cost to the firm, since establishments cannibalize each other's demand. We show that uniform pricing across a firm's establishments is optimal. The unique equilibrium involves price distributions with supports connected and nested by firm size: larger firms post prices over a wider support but earn lower profit per establishment. Finally, mergers can increase concentration while reducing expected transaction prices and markups when the merger does not create a new market leader. When the merger creates a new largest firm, its effect can instead reverse, depending on the relative strength of the concentration and largest-firm channels. Thus, the effect of greater concentration depends critically on how ownership changes the firm size distribution.

detail.abstract: Over 1.1 billion people live in informal settlements. Although these communities are ubiquitous in low-income countries and rare in high-income countries, their prevalence varies widely across middle-income countries. However, a phenomenon that has received little theoretical or empirical attention is how informal settlements could become more common in a country where they previously had been declining. We argue that one way this can occur is when social shocks embolden land invasions while reducing formal and informal capacity to stop them. We test this theory by studying Chile's 2019 social unrest. Using a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods, we find that the rate at which these communities formed increased approximately fourfold during the crisis. We also find that some of the founders of these settlements believed that the unrest made their claims to invade land more legitimate and that the government and surrounding community would not intervene.

detail.abstract: We study the interaction between bank payouts and creditors' rollover decisions in a dynamic model where a public liquidity facility can temporarily replace funding withdrawn by non-rolling creditors. We solve the model in closed form and characterize how shareholders' payout policy and creditors' rollover behavior are jointly determined in equilibrium and vary with the reliability of liquidity support. A more reliable facility encourages debt rollover but also induces earlier payouts and smaller buffers, partially offsetting its stabilizing effect. We show that dividend restrictions counteract this feedback, reducing rollover risk and increasing firm value. Their effectiveness is nonmonotonic in the facility reliability, while the optimal restriction becomes less stringent as reliability increases. When recapitalization is endogenous, however, sufficiently tight restrictions eliminate incentives to recapitalize, limiting how aggressively payouts can be restricted.

detail.abstract: One remarkable feature that has contributed to the durability of the United States Constitution is its scientific neutrality. There is no Constitutionally-mandated version of chemistry, biology, physics, or even sciences of human nature such as psychology or anthropology. As a result, it is consistent with all of them. For the most part, all have been able to develop free of excessive interference from judges interpreting the Constitution. One powerful and distressing exception to the Constitution's scientific neutrality is the way that the Supreme Court has interpreted economics. The Constitution has been read in the past and increasingly once again today as embodying a particularly "classical" view of economics. The classical view of political economy encompasses strong property and contract rights, an idea that judges should do little more than act as umpires in disputes, and business decisions that are disciplined mainly by the market. It is highly suspicious of government economic regulation and commensurately suspicious of regulatory agencies. In accordance with that, it assumes that the three Articles of the Constitution establishing the legislative (Art. I), executive (Art. II), and judicial (Art. III) powers are not merely the Constitution's way of organizing its text, but that they also establish rigid lines that the various branches cannot cross. Economics, just as any science, does not stand still. Significant changes occurred from the late nineteenth century on. In industry and manufacturing it was the rise of big business, driven heavily by a technological revolution, and the enormous growth of the labor market. In economic theory, the most notable development was the marginalist revolution. For any other science the Constitution would have stood aside and let the legislative policy chips fall where they may. But that has not been the result for economics where, first in the Substantive Due Process era of the early twentieth century and again today the Supreme Court is marching to a different economic drummer than the rest of the country.

detail.abstract: The taxation of carried interests has been one of the hottest topics in the tax world for the last 15 years with the issue first raised over 30 years ago. A number of tax scholars have proposed various alternatives to the current tax regime for carried interests with little agreement on the proper taxation of such interests. In addition, over the last 30 years, tax scholars have made a number of breakthroughs in understanding the taxation of supernormal returns, sometimes referred to as excess profits. The income or profits associated with a carried interest appears to be a classic example of supernormal returns. As a result, applying our relatively newfound understanding of supernormal returns to the taxation of carried interests can unlock the key to the proper taxation of such interests and solve a decades- old mystery.

detail.abstract: Environmental pollution remains a critical challenge in developing countries. This paper thus investigates the relationship between corporate sustainability engagement and the environmental conditions of the districts in which firms operate across districts in India. Operationalising organisational websites, we apply deep learning methods to construct firm-level sustainability engagement scores and aggregate them to the district level. We combine these indicators with earth-observation measures of air pollution and vegetation and estimate district-level regressions using spatial lag models to account for spatial dependencies. We find that more polluted districts host more sustainability-engaged firms in absolute terms. Yet, this association is largely absorbed by industrial concentration, population density, and institutional quality once controls are included. The relative share of sustainability-engaged firms shows no significant relationship with air quality. The study highlights the potential of large-scale web text analysis combined with complementary geodata for examining environmental sustainability engagement. A key limitation is the low availability of firm-level data, highlighting the need for improved data infrastructure for environmental and sustainability research in emerging economies.

detail.abstract: We study a self-reinforcing information problem arising from two-way learning between central bank and financial markets. When policy is difficult to predict, market participants trade less aggressively on their private information, so prices reveal less about economic conditions. Poor price signals then make it harder to learn how policy responds to those conditions. This feedback can sustain both low-and high-information regimes separated by an unstable threshold, even though the equilibrium is uniquely pinned down. In a low-information trap, policy uncertainty persists alongside uninformative asset prices. The model also provides a dynamic perspective on the reflection problem: when the market learns about the central bank's reaction function, the central bank's reliance on market prices can strengthen subsequent price informativeness. This market's learning channel provides an additional mechanism through which policy decision shape the asset price informativeness.

detail.abstract: Patents let pharmaceutical firms price new therapeutics largely free from competitive constraint. Outside the U.S., value-based pricing (VBP) ties market access and price to evidence of therapeutic benefit or cost-effectiveness after regulatory approval. This paper examines what VBP does to pharmaceutical market value: how much the owner can capture, which R&D directions get funded, and whether an unfavorable decision destroys or merely delays value realization. We compare structurally different VBP models: Germany's added health benefit system and England's cost-effectiveness threshold. We test their effect on market value using stock market reactions to reimbursement decisions for publicly listed firms, 2000-2025. Neither favorable nor unfavorable VBP decisions move stock prices in either country: investors do not treat them as new information about firm value. The null result implies how little VBP threatens the incentive to innovate, and how firms and policymakers should weigh reimbursement risk against patent-driven return expectations.

detail.abstract: Regulatory forbearance is a fiscal transfer. Insolvent borrowers survive only as long as the government can afford to stand behind the banks that carry their loans, so their equity should load on the sovereign's capacity to backstop its banking system. I show that this exposure is priced. In Japan, an intermediary leverage factor prices portfolios of zombie firms but not the broad cross-section. Decomposing it, what prices zombies is the sovereign risk component of intermediary risk, while the orthogonal component prices bank-dependent firms that are not necessarily zombies. After the November 1997 failures that tested the government's backstop, zombies underperformed other firms. When support is direct rather than intermediated, the same exposure is priced without banks. I show that a U.S. sovereign risk factor prices portfolios of federal government suppliers, which underperformed after the 2011 downgrade.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) changes the architecture of information production by routing information producers' analysis through the same foundation models and public information sources, potentially reducing information diversity. In this study, we examine this possibility using financial analysts' earnings forecasts. We document that following the public release of ChatGPT, forecast divergence falls sharply while consensus forecast accuracy improves. Using a classifier that detects AI-assisted content in analyst research reports, we find that the decline in forecast divergence is concentrated in firm-quarters whose analyst reports show stronger evidence of AI assistance. Analyst reports covering the same firm-quarter also become more textually similar. A further decomposition of forecast errors suggests greater correlation across analysts' errors, with no significant decline in total forecast uncertainty. Additional analyses reveal that corporate investment becomes less sensitive to Tobin's Q. Together, these findings suggest reduced diversity in the information underlying analysts' forecasts.

detail.abstract: This report examines standard-essential patent (SEP) litigation before the Unified Patent Court (UPC) during its first three years of operation, from 1 June 2023 to 30 June 2026. Of 515 infringement actions, 112 (21.7%) involve at least one identified SEP. These cases concentrate in cellular technologies (58.9%), followed by video coding and networking, and in German local divisions, which hear 92.0% of SEP actions against 73.9% of non-SEP actions. A small group of claimants accounts for much of the activity, and firms active in both product and technology markets are the largest claimant group (70.9%). Enforcement targets mainly the downstream end of the value chain: final-product manufacturers (61.0%) and distributors and retailers (25.4%), with component suppliers only 4.2%. Among actions with an observed outcome, 83.7% ended without a judgment on the merits.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Evidence-based policymaking (EBPM) took its name from evidence-based medicine and is now studied both in health research and in public administration. This short report maps its literature in PubMed and Scopus in parallel to trace how far it has grown beyond medicine and how much a PubMed-only analysis would miss.
Methods: Records with “evidence-based policy” or “evidence-informed policy” and their variants in the title or abstract were retrieved from PubMed and Scopus (1990–2025). After records published in 2026 were removed, 3,058 PubMed and 6,480 Scopus records remained. Records were matched by PubMed identifier and, failing that, by DOI. Scopus records in medicine, nursing, and health professions were retrieved separately to measure the coverage of PubMed. Both sets were analyzed with bibliometrix in R.
Results: In the indexed literature, EBPM first appeared and grew in medicine: all ten Scopus records of 1994–1997 were in the medical subject areas, and the first records in public administration journals appeared in 1998 and 1999. The share of records in PubMed fell to 45% in 1999–2008 and 43% in 2018–2025, and the share of Scopus records in the medical subject areas fell from 51% to 38%, while the number of health records kept rising. Of the 6,931 distinct records, 2,599 were in both databases, 459 only in PubMed, and 3,873 only in Scopus. PubMed contained 81.6% of the 2,680 Scopus records in the medical subject areas; the 492 it lacked included 106 books and book chapters. Records only in Scopus came mainly from policy, public administration, and environmental journals, and they included the most locally cited works from public administration. Both databases grew sharply in 2025. “Evidence-informed” appeared in about one in five records indexed in both databases after 2009, but in fewer than one in ten records indexed only in Scopus. With affiliation countries recomputed, the United Kingdom ranked close to the United States in both databases.
Conclusion: In the indexed literature, EBPM grew alongside evidence-based medicine in medical journals in the 1990s and later spread beyond medicine, to public administration and the other social sciences, where most of its literature now lies. For EBPM in health, PubMed alone covers most of the indexed literature; for the concept as a whole, it holds less than half, and a second database is needed.

detail.abstract: Financial advisors increasingly delegate portfolio construction to model portfolios, which now guide an estimated $9.3 trillion in U.S. advised assets. The allocation of retail capital across funds is thus shifting from advisors' dispersed judgment toward these centralized investment rules. I study how model portfolios affect capital allocation and whether their diffusion changes fund managers' incentives to compete for capital and to actively seek profit opportunities. I find that models are a significant and contrarian driver of fund flows: the rebalancing toward their target weights buffers funds against performance-driven outflows, but also dampens the reward for outperformance. Accordingly, funds more exposed to model recommendations take less risk after poor performance and show weaker performance persistence. Overall, the stability provided by the models spares investors part of the losses from poorly timed flows, but at the cost of weaker incentives for effort among fund managers exposed to these recommendations.

detail.abstract: The Mewes Strategy, historically known as the Engpasskonzentrierte Strategie (EKS), or Bottleneck-Concentrated Strategy, is a distinctive approach to strategic focus. It directs a firm's capabilities towards the minimum factor that currently constrains the development of a defined target group and seeks to generate superior customer utility through concentrated problem solving. The approach is explicitly dynamic: its implementation phases are to be revisited, bottlenecks are to be reexamined , innovation is to be driven by customer problems, and long-term specialisation is linked to a constant underlying need. From this perspective, three lifecycle levels become visible: the lifecycle of the bottleneck solution, the lifecycle of the bottleneck itself, and the lifecycle of the system architecture that generates the bottleneck. Corporate Viability extends bottleneck fit by asking whether the firm can recognise and cross the boundary between those system states. Long-term viability therefore depends on Re-Fit Capability: the capacity to recreate strategic fit when the original bottleneck, business model or market architecture no longer provides a viable basis for the future.

detail.abstract: Frontier AI models, which are the small class of the most advanced general purpose AI models, have become a central object of both international cooperation and geopolitical competition. The European Union (EU) and the United States (US) have both developed dedicated governance frameworks for the frontier. Their background conditions are ones that the policy convergence literature associates with convergence, yet their approaches differ substantially, with the EU relying on binding regulation enforced by a centralised institution, while the US relies on executive instruments and voluntary commitments that have changed considerably between administrations. This article asks along which dimensions the two approaches converge, through which mechanisms, and why convergence stops at binding authority. It conceptualises convergence along three dimensions: problem definition, regulatory technology and enforcement authority, and finds sustained convergence on the technical layer, partial convergence on the conceptual layer and divergence on the institutional layer. The study identifies transnational communication through epistemic communities as one of the strongest mechanisms of convergence.

detail.abstract: How does foreign direct investment affect domestic product quality? Exploiting FDI liberalization across Indian manufacturing industries, we find that domestic product quality declines on average, but this masks sharply heterogeneous responses. Domestic firms substantially below the quality of foreign competitors upgrade following liberalization, while those near or above foreign quality downgrade. We provide evidence for a new mechanism operating through the competition channel: foreign firms occupy an intermediate position on the quality ladder and charge prices comparable to high-quality domestic producers. Greater exposure to such competitors may therefore reduce the returns to maintaining quality substantially above the foreign benchmark, reinforcing competitive pressures to downgrade. Our findings show that domestic firms’ quality responses to foreign entry depend critically on their position relative to foreign competitors.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) could sustain research productivity if they lower the cost of combining distant ideas across an ever-expanding knowledge space. We develop a model of idea search linking research productivity with the extent of a researcher's knowledge frontier, and we test its central prediction on 21.9 million journal articles published between 2018 and 2025. Using a purpose-trained detector of LLM-generated text, we find LLM usage in 40% of abstracts by October 2025, including 31% of abstracts in top journals. Papers with LLM-assisted abstracts draw on more unusual combinations of prior work: 61% of flagged papers are tail-novel, against 54% of unflagged ones. A staggered difference-indifferences design compares publications before and after each researcher's first flagged paper and finds that AI adoption is linked with increased novelty and originality within researcher careers. We find a 6% increase in uncommon term combinations and a 4.5% increase in forward disruption, as well as a 9% increase in the probability of reaching the top 10% of citations.
